pages.question: A 45-year-old male construction worker presents to the clinic with persistent pain in his left wrist after twisting it while operating heavy machinery two days ago. He denies any fall but reports immediate pain and swelling. On examination, there is tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox and pain with axial loading of the thumb. Initial radiographs show no evidence of fracture or dislocation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text: Apply a short arm cast without thumb involvement
Discharge with oral analgesics and activity modification without immobilization
Order an immediate MRI of the wrist
Apply a thumb spica splint and repeat radiographs in 10 days

pages.question: A 45-year-old male construction worker presents to the clinic with persistent pain in his left wrist after twisting it while operating heavy machinery two days ago. He denies any fall but reports immediate pain and swelling. On examination, there is tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox and pain with axial loading of the thumb. Initial radiographs show no evidence of fracture or dislocation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Apply a short arm cast without thumb involvement
(6.06%)

Discharge with oral analgesics and activity modification without immobilization
(12.12%)

Order an immediate MRI of the wrist
(7.58%)

Apply a thumb spica splint and repeat radiographs in 10 days
(74.24%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's mechanism of injury (wrist twisting) and clinical findings (anatomic snuffbox tenderness, pain with axial thumb loading) are classic for scaphoid fracture. Even with negative initial radiographs, up to 15% of scaphoid fractures may not be visible on initial imaging. Due to the scaphoid's retrograde blood supply and risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole, immediate immobilization with a thumb spica splint is essential, followed by repeat radiographs in 7-10 days to detect fractures that become radiographically apparent.
(Choice A)
Apply a short arm cast without thumb involvement
This is inadequate because scaphoid fractures require immobilization that includes the thumb and extends to the interphalangeal joint (thumb spica). A short arm cast without thumb involvement fails to adequately immobilize the scaphoid bone and may lead to displacement or nonunion.
(Choice B)
Perform immediate surgical fixation
Surgery is not indicated for suspected nondisplaced fractures without confirmation; conservative management with immobilization is preferred initially.
(Choice C)
Discharge with oral analgesics and activity modification without immobilization
This is incorrect because suspected scaphoid fractures require immobilization even with negative initial radiographs. The scaphoid's retrograde blood supply makes it vulnerable to avascular necrosis and nonunion if a fracture is missed and left untreated.
(Choice D)
Order an immediate MRI of the wrist
While MRI can detect occult scaphoid fractures with high sensitivity, it is not the most appropriate initial step. Current evidence-based guidelines recommend immobilization with thumb spica splint and repeat radiographs in 7-10 days as the first-line approach, reserving MRI for cases where repeat radiographs remain negative but clinical suspicion persists.
(Choice E)
Apply a thumb spica splint and repeat radiographs in 10 days
This is the appropriate initial management for suspected scaphoid fracture with negative x-rays, allowing time for the fracture to become visible while preventing complications like avascular necrosis.

pages.question: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, presents to her primary care physician 4 months after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of her first child. She describes a soft, painless swelling in the central abdomen that becomes more prominent when she performs sit-ups or lifts her baby. She has no history of abdominal surgery, denies constipation, nausea, or vomiting, and reports normal bowel movements. Physical examination reveals a 3-cm wide, nontender midline bulge above the umbilicus that is accentuated by having the patient raise her head while supine, with intact overlying skin and no palpable fascial defect. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Computed tomography scan of the abdomen
(0%)

Immediate surgical plication of the rectus muscles
(5.56%)

Referral to physical therapy for core strengthening exercises
(25%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has rectus abdominis diastasis, presenting as a nontender midline abdominal bulge due to weakening of the linea alba without fascial disruption or obstructive symptoms. Conservative management with observation and reassurance is indicated, with surgical options considered only if symptoms persist well beyond the postpartum period.
(Choice A)
Prescription of an abdominal binder
Abdominal binders may provide temporary cosmetic improvement and comfort but do not treat the underlying condition. They are not routinely recommended as first-line management for uncomplicated rectus diastasis, especially when the patient is asymptomatic.
(Choice B)
Computed tomography scan of the abdomen
CT imaging is unnecessary for rectus diastasis, which is diagnosed clinically by the characteristic midline bulge that becomes prominent with Valsalva maneuvers. The absence of a palpable fascial defect and lack of concerning symptoms make imaging inappropriate.
(Choice C)
Immediate surgical plication of the rectus muscles
Surgical intervention is premature at 4 months postpartum for rectus diastasis. Surgery is typically reserved for cases that remain symptomatic or cosmetically bothersome after at least 12 months postpartum when natural healing is complete and conservative measures have failed.
(Choice D)
Referral to physical therapy for core strengthening exercises
While physical therapy with core strengthening exercises may help improve symptoms and appearance over time, it is not the most appropriate initial step. The primary management is observation since many cases resolve spontaneously. PT referral would be considered if the patient desires active intervention or has functional limitations.
(Choice E)
Observation and reassurance
This is the correct management for rectus abdominis diastasis in the postpartum period, as it often resolves spontaneously with time and does not require immediate intervention unless symptomatic or persistent.

pages.question:
A 3-day-old female infant presents to the pediatric clinic with symptoms of excessive crying, poor weight gain, and episodes of diarrhea. The infant was born at 38 weeks gestation via uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a 28-year-old mother with a history of Graves' disease, which was managed with subtotal thyroidectomy 18 months prior to pregnancy. The mother has been on stable levothyroxine replacement therapy and remained euthyroid during pregnancy without any antithyroid medications. Physical examination reveals a heart rate of 180 beats per minute, warm and moist skin, mild exophthalmos, and a palpable thyroid gland. Laboratory values are shown below. What is the most likely mechanism responsible for this infant's presentation?



WBC Count	7300 /µL
Neutrophils	59 %
Lymphocytes	31 %
Hemoglobin	13.6 g/dL
Hematocrit	40.5 %
RBC Count	4.6 million/µL
Platelet Count	245000 /µL
Free T4	3.2 ng/dL
Total T3	310 ng/dL
TSH	<0.01 mU/L
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)	14 mg/dL
Serum Creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
Estimated GFR	>90 mL/min/1.73 m²
Serum Sodium	138 mEq/L
Serum Potassium	4.1 mEq/L
AST (SGOT)	27 U/L
ALT (SGPT)	31 U/L
Albumin	4.3 g/dL
Total Protein	7.1 g/dL

answers.text:
Transplacental passage of TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies
(81.93%)

Maternal iodine deficiency causing compensatory neonatal hyperthyroidism
(0%)

Activating TSH receptor gene mutation causing McCune-Albright syndrome
(1.2%)

Autoimmune destruction of the infant's thyroid gland
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Neonatal thyrotoxicosis resulting from transplacental passage of maternal thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) or TRAb (TSH-receptor antibodies), leading to hyperstimulation of the infant's thyroid gland and excessive thyroid hormone production. This can occur even in mothers who are euthyroid post-thyroidectomy for Graves' disease, as these antibodies may persist for years after treatment. Clinical features include tachycardia, irritability, poor feeding, failure to thrive, diarrhea, exophthalmos, and goiter. The condition is typically transient, resolving over 2-3 months as maternal antibodies are metabolized and cleared from the infant's circulation.
(Choice A)
Transplacental passage of TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies
This is the correct mechanism; maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and stimulate the fetal thyroid, causing hyperthyroidism in the neonate, independent of the mother's current thyroid status.
(Choice B)
Maternal iodine deficiency causing compensatory neonatal hyperthyroidism
This is incorrect; iodine deficiency typically leads to hypothyroidism or goiter without hyperthyroidism, and is not linked to maternal Graves' disease.
(Choice C)
Activating TSH receptor gene mutation causing McCune-Albright syndrome
This is incorrect; while activating TSH receptor mutations can cause neonatal hyperthyroidism, they are extremely rare, typically present as part of McCune-Albright syndrome, and would not be associated with maternal Graves' disease history or the transient course expected here.
(Choice D)
Transplacental passage of antithyroid drugs
This is incorrect; the mother was not on antithyroid medications during pregnancy as she had undergone thyroidectomy and was on levothyroxine replacement. Additionally, transplacental passage of antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil) would cause fetal/neonatal hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism.
(Choice E)
Autoimmune destruction of the infant's thyroid gland
This is incorrect; autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue (as seen in neonatal Hashimoto's thyroiditis) would cause hypothyroidism with elevated TSH, not the hyperthyroid picture with suppressed TSH seen in this infant. The clinical presentation and laboratory findings are consistent with thyroid stimulation, not destruction.

pages.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with sudden-onset coughing, wheezing, and difficulty breathing that began during his birthday party. The parents report that he was eating cake and playing with popped balloon fragments shortly before the symptoms started. On examination, the child is in moderate respiratory distress with decreased breath sounds over the left lung field. A chest x-ray reveals hyperinflation of the left lung with mediastinal shift to the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's sudden-onset respiratory distress with unilateral hyperinflation and mediastinal shift on x-ray are indicative of foreign body aspiration, most common in young children. Clinical features include acute cough, dyspnea, and asymmetric breath sounds. Rigid bronchoscopy is the preferred method for diagnosis and removal of the aspirated object in children. Other options are inappropriate as they treat alternative diagnoses like asthma, infection, or mucus plugging without addressing the foreign body.
(Choice A)
Flexible bronchoscopy
Flexible bronchoscopy can visualize the foreign body but has limited ability to remove objects in pediatric patients due to smaller working channel and less rigid suction capabilities compared to rigid bronchoscopy.
(Choice B)
Rigid bronchoscopy
Rigid bronchoscopy is the gold standard for both diagnosis and removal of aspirated foreign bodies in children, allowing for airway control and extraction.
(Choice C)
Chest physiotherapy
Chest physiotherapy helps mobilize secretions in conditions like cystic fibrosis or pneumonia but cannot dislodge a solid foreign body causing complete or partial airway obstruction.
(Choice D)
Nebulized albuterol
Nebulized albuterol treats bronchospasm in conditions like asthma or reactive airway disease but does not address the underlying mechanical obstruction from an aspirated foreign body.
(Choice E)
CT scan of the chest
While CT scan would provide detailed imaging and could confirm foreign body location, it delays definitive management in a child with clear clinical signs of foreign body aspiration requiring immediate intervention.

pages.question:
A 58-year-old woman with a history of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)-related cirrhosis presents to the emergency department with progressive abdominal distension, leg swelling, and decreased urine output over the past week. She has been compliant with her diuretic regimen of spironolactone 100 mg daily and furosemide 40 mg daily. Two days ago, she experienced a mild upper gastrointestinal bleed that resolved spontaneously. Physical examination reveals jaundice, tense ascites, and pitting edema in the lower extremities. Laboratory results are shown below. Ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis, and there is no evidence of ongoing infection or nephrotoxic medication use. What is the most likely mechanism underlying her acute kidney injury?



White Blood Cell Count (WBC)	7.4×109/L
Red Blood Cell Count (RBC)	4.85×1012/L
Hemoglobin (Hgb)	14.3 g/dL
Serum Creatinine	2.8 mg/dL
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)	45 mg/dL
Serum Sodium	128 mEq/L

Urine Sodium	8 mEq/L	(range:> 20mEq/L)
Urine Protein	Negative
Urine Blood	Negative
Urine Sediment	Bland (No casts or cells)

answers.text:
Acute tubular necrosis secondary to ischemic injury
(21.88%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient with advanced cirrhosis presents with hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), a form of functional acute kidney injury characterized by renal hypoperfusion. The diagnosis is supported by: cirrhosis with portal hypertension, precipitating factors (GI bleed, diuretics), very low urine sodium (<10 mEq/L), bland urine sediment, and absence of structural kidney disease. HRS results from splanchnic vasodilation leading to effective arterial hypovolemia and compensatory renal vasoconstriction. Management includes discontinuing diuretics, treating precipitants, careful volume expansion with albumin, and vasoconstrictor therapy (terlipressin, or midodrine/octreotide combination).
(Choice A)
Renal hypoperfusion
Hepatorenal syndrome causes functional renal failure due to intense renal vasoconstriction secondary to splanchnic vasodilation and effective hypovolemia in cirrhosis, leading to hypoperfusion without structural kidney damage.
(Choice B)
Acute tubular necrosis secondary to ischemic injury
Acute tubular necrosis typically presents with muddy brown casts in the urine sediment and urine sodium >20 mEq/L. While the recent GI bleed could theoretically cause ischemic ATN, the very low urine sodium (8 mEq/L) and bland sediment indicate preserved tubular function with pre-renal azotemia rather than structural tubular damage.
(Choice C)
Obstructive nephropathy
Obstructive nephropathy is excluded by the normal ultrasound showing no hydronephrosis. Additionally, obstruction typically causes higher urine sodium levels once the obstruction is established, unlike the very low sodium (8 mEq/L) seen here.
(Choice D)
Acute glomerulonephritis
Glomerulonephritis would present with an active urine sediment including proteinuria, hematuria, and red blood cell casts. The bland sediment with negative protein and blood makes glomerular disease highly unlikely.
(Choice E)
Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis
There is no evidence of nephrotoxic medication exposure, and drug-induced nephritis typically presents with active urine sediment including eosinophils or white cell casts. The clinical presentation of cirrhosis with ascites, low urine sodium, and bland sediment is classic for hepatorenal syndrome.

pages.question: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with newly diagnosed metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer. She has no significant past medical history and is asymptomatic from a cardiac standpoint. Her oncologist plans to initiate targeted therapy with trastuzumab in combination with pertuzumab and docetaxel. Which of the following baseline evaluations is most essential prior to starting this regimen?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Trastuzumab carries a well-established risk of cardiotoxicity, particularly a decrease in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) that may progress to congestive heart failure. This risk is heightened when combined with anthracyclines (doxorubicin, epirubicin) or in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease. Current guidelines mandate baseline echocardiography or MUGA scan to assess LVEF before starting trastuzumab, with periodic monitoring every 3 months during treatment. The other baseline evaluations listed (audiometry, bone density, bone marrow biopsy, Factor V Leiden testing, pulmonary function testing, and tuberculosis screening) are not routinely required for trastuzumab initiation as they address toxicities not associated with HER2-targeted therapy.
(Choice A)
Bone density measurement
Bone density measurement is relevant for patients on aromatase inhibitors or those at risk for osteoporosis, but it is not required prior to trastuzumab therapy.
(Choice B)
Echocardiography
Echocardiography is essential to establish baseline cardiac function due to trastuzumab's risk of cardiotoxicity, allowing for monitoring of left ventricular ejection fraction during therapy.
(Choice C)
Tuberculosis skin testing
Tuberculosis screening is required before initiating immunosuppressive therapies like TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) or high-dose corticosteroids that increase infection risk. Trastuzumab is a targeted therapy that does not significantly suppress immune function.
(Choice D)
Pulmonary function testing
Pulmonary function testing is indicated for drugs with pulmonary toxicity, such as bleomycin, but trastuzumab does not require this baseline evaluation.
(Choice E)
Factor V Leiden testing
Factor V Leiden testing assesses inherited thrombophilia risk. While some cancer therapies like tamoxifen or bevacizumab may increase thrombotic risk, trastuzumab does not significantly increase clotting risk and does not require baseline thrombophilia screening.

pages.question: A 63-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of intermittent episodes of upper abdominal pain radiating to his back. The pain is often associated with bloating and is exacerbated after consuming fatty meals, persisting for approximately two hours. He reports this discomfort has increased in frequency over the last six months. Physical examination reveals mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant, but there is no guarding or rebound tenderness. Routine blood tests and a chest X-ray are unremarkable. An abdominal ultrasound shows an irregular, echogenic structure in the gallbladder wall, suggesting calcification. Which condition is this patient at the greatest risk for developing?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The presence of a 'porcelain gallbladder,' characterized by calcification of the gallbladder wall seen on ultrasound, significantly increases the risk of gallbladder carcinoma. This calcification results from chronic inflammation and is considered a premalignant condition. Current guidelines recommend prophylactic cholecystectomy due to the 12-60% risk of malignant transformation, making surgical evaluation urgent.
(Choice A)
Acute cholecystitis
Acute cholecystitis typically results from gallstone obstruction of the cystic duct causing inflammation, not from gallbladder wall calcification. While this patient has right upper quadrant tenderness, the absence of fever, leukocytosis, and Murphy's sign makes acute cholecystitis unlikely. The porcelain gallbladder finding is specifically associated with malignancy risk, not acute inflammatory conditions.
(Choice B)
Peptic ulcer disease
While peptic ulcer disease can cause upper abdominal pain that radiates to the back, it is not associated with gallbladder wall calcification. PUD typically presents with epigastric pain related to meals and is caused by H. pylori infection or NSAIDs, not gallbladder pathology. The ultrasound finding of gallbladder wall calcification is pathognomonic for porcelain gallbladder, which carries malignancy risk.
(Choice C)
Gallbladder carcinoma
A calcified, or 'porcelain' gallbladder, indicates a significant risk for gallbladder carcinoma. The calcification in the gallbladder's wall is a known risk factor for malignant transformation, warranting further surgical assessment.

pages.question: A 32-year-old male landscaper presents with several skin lesions on his hands and forearms that developed over the past 3 days. He reports that the lesions began as small, fragile blisters that rapidly enlarged and filled with yellow fluid. Some blisters have ruptured, leaving behind moist, crusted areas with a distinctive thin, scaly rim at the edges. He denies fever, systemic symptoms, or recent travel. Physical examination reveals flaccid bullae with serous yellow fluid and peripheral collarettes of scale on ruptured lesions. Gram stain of the fluid shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's presentation of enlarging flaccid bullae filled with yellow fluid on the hands and forearms, with ruptured lesions showing a collarette of scale, is consistent with bullous impetigo, which is caused by Staphylococcus aureus producing exfoliative toxins.
(Choice A)
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is the primary cause of bullous impetigo, producing exfoliative toxins that lead to the formation of flaccid bullae filled with yellow fluid, which rupture to leave a collarette of scale.
(Choice B)
Trichophyton rubrum
Trichophyton rubrum causes tinea corporis with annular plaques and scaling, but not fluid-filled bullae that rupture to form collarettes.
(Choice C)
Candida albicans
Candida albicans is a yeast that would show budding yeasts and pseudohyphae on microscopy, not gram-positive cocci in clusters. It typically causes intertrigo in moist areas with satellite pustules, not the large flaccid bullae described.
(Choice D)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative rod, not gram-positive cocci in clusters. It can cause ecthyma gangrenosum with necrotic ulcers or folliculitis in hot tub exposure, but not the characteristic flaccid bullae with yellow fluid seen in bullous impetigo.
(Choice E)
Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus pyogenes typically causes non-bullous impetigo with honey-crusted lesions and would show gram-positive cocci in chains, not clusters. It does not produce the exfoliative toxins that create flaccid bullae with collarettes of scale.

pages.question: A mother brings her 7-year-old son to his pediatrician with concerns that he refuses to eat at school lunch, eats only at home, and has lost 2 kg over the past 3 months. She describes him as anxious about "what might be in the food" and worried he might choke or vomit at school. He had one episode of vomiting at school 4 months ago and has refused to eat outside the home since. His weight is now at the 10th percentile, down from the 40th. He has no sensory sensitivities, no body image concerns, and no food texture aversions. He accepts a wide variety of foods at home. A review of systems is otherwise negative. Which of the following is the most accurate characterization of this child's condition?

answers.text:
Separation anxiety disorder manifesting as school refusal with secondary food restriction
(0%)

Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, fear-of-aversive-consequences subtype
(100%)

Normal developmental feeding behavior that will resolve without intervention
(0%)

Specific phobia requiring immediate psychiatric hospitalization
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This child has the fear-of-aversive-consequences subtype of ARFID, in which food refusal is driven by anxiety about choking, vomiting, or illness rather than sensory properties or lack of interest. This subtype requires referral to behavioral psychology for cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) targeting the conditioned fear response, in addition to nutritional support. Distinguishing this subtype from sensory-based ARFID and normal picky eating guides appropriate therapy referral.
(Choice A)
Separation anxiety disorder manifesting as school refusal with secondary food restriction
Separation anxiety disorder involves excessive distress about separation from caregivers across multiple contexts and situations. This child's anxiety is specifically limited to eating outside the home following a discrete traumatic event (vomiting episode), not generalized separation concerns or school avoidance. The specificity of the fear to eating behavior and clear precipitating event make ARFID the primary diagnosis.
(Choice B)
Anorexia nervosa with atypical presentation
Anorexia nervosa requires distorted body image and/or intense fear of weight gain as central features, neither of which is present here. This child's food restriction is driven by fear of vomiting and choking, not by a desire to lose weight or alter his body. ARFID and anorexia nervosa are distinct diagnoses in DSM-5, and correctly distinguishing them is essential for appropriate treatment planning.
(Choice C)
Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, fear-of-aversive-consequences subtype
ARFID encompasses three recognized subtypes: (1) sensory sensitivity (avoidance based on texture, color, smell), (2) lack of interest in eating (low appetite, poor hunger drive), and (3) fear of aversive consequences (avoidance driven by fear of choking, vomiting, or allergic reaction). This child's food refusal is clearly linked to a conditioned fear following an aversive vomiting episode at school, resulting in context-specific restriction — he eats normally at home where he feels safe. The absence of sensory aversions, body image disturbance, or lack of appetite further supports the fear-based subtype. The significant weight loss and functional impairment (inability to eat at school) confirm the ARFID diagnosis. This subtype is best managed with referral to behavioral psychology for cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which targets the conditioned fear response through graduated exposure and cognitive restructuring. Nutritional support and communication with school staff may also be warranted during treatment.
(Choice D)
Normal developmental feeding behavior that will resolve without intervention
Normal developmental feeding preferences involve mild food selectivity but do not cause significant weight loss (this child dropped from 40th to 10th percentile), functional impairment (inability to eat at school), or context-dependent restriction tied to specific feared outcomes. This degree of weight loss and functional limitation requires clinical evaluation and intervention, not expectant management.
(Choice E)
Specific phobia requiring immediate psychiatric hospitalization
While this child demonstrates fear-based food avoidance, psychiatric hospitalization is reserved for cases with severe malnutrition, medical instability, or failure of outpatient interventions. This child's weight at the 10th percentile, while concerning, does not indicate immediate medical crisis. The appropriate initial approach is outpatient referral to behavioral psychology for cognitive-behavioral therapy targeting the conditioned fear response.

pages.question:
A 62-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 3-day history of increasing fatigue, shortness of breath on exertion, and dark-colored urine. He reports yellowing of his skin and eyes. Two weeks ago, he was treated with intravenous cefazolin for a skin and soft tissue infection following a minor surgical procedure. He has no history of blood disorders or allergies. Physical examination reveals jaundice, pallor, and mild splenomegaly. Laboratory studies are shown below. What is the best next step in management?



Hemoglobin	8.2 g/dL
Hematocrit	25 %
Red Blood Cell Count	2.8 million/μL
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)	92 fL
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)	31 pg
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)	34 g/dL
White Blood Cell Count (WBC)	8.0 ×10^9/L
Neutrophils	60 %
Lymphocytes	30 %
Monocytes	6 %
Eosinophils	3 %
Basophils	1 %
Platelet Count	240 ×10^9/L
Reticulocyte Count	8 %
Total Bilirubin	3.5 mg/dL
Indirect (Unconjugated) Bilirubin	3.0 mg/dL
Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test	Positive
Peripheral Smear	Spherocytes observed
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This 62-year-old man developed symptoms of fatigue, exertional dyspnea, dark urine, and jaundice after receiving cefazolin, consistent with drug-induced immune-mediated hemolytic anemia. Key findings include anemia with reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, positive Coombs test, and splenomegaly. The best management is to discontinue the offending drug (cefazolin), which typically leads to resolution.
(Choice A)
Start erythropoietin injections
Erythropoietin stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow and is primarily used for anemias due to decreased production (such as chronic kidney disease or chemotherapy-induced anemia). In acute hemolytic anemia, the bone marrow is already responding appropriately with increased reticulocyte production (8% in this case), so erythropoietin would not be beneficial.
(Choice B)
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin
IVIG is primarily used for immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and certain other autoimmune conditions. While it may have some benefit in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, it is not first-line therapy for drug-induced hemolytic anemia where discontinuing the offending medication is the most effective and immediate intervention.
(Choice C)
Discontinue cefazolin
Cefazolin is the likely trigger for this immune-mediated extravascular hemolytic anemia, and discontinuation typically results in rapid resolution of hemolysis.
(Choice D)
Order bone marrow biopsy
Bone marrow biopsy is indicated when there is concern for primary bone marrow pathology or when the cause of anemia is unclear. In this case, the clinical presentation (post-antibiotic exposure), laboratory findings (positive Coombs test, spherocytes, elevated reticulocytes), and indirect hyperbilirubinemia clearly point to drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia, making bone marrow evaluation unnecessary.
(Choice E)
Perform red blood cell transfusion
While this patient has symptomatic anemia (fatigue, dyspnea), red blood cell transfusion should be reserved for severe anemia or hemodynamic instability. More importantly, transfusion does not address the ongoing hemolytic process and may be less effective if the underlying cause continues. Discontinuing cefazolin stops the hemolysis at its source.

pages.question: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after falling from a second-story balcony while intoxicated. She landed on her chest and complains of severe chest pain. Vital signs show blood pressure of 85/55 mm Hg, heart rate of 118 bpm, and respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min. She remains hypotensive despite administration of 3 liters of intravenous crystalloid fluids. Central venous pressure is 16 mm Hg. Electrocardiogram reveals sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST-segment changes. Chest x-ray is unremarkable, and bedside ultrasound shows no evidence of pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pericardial effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.text:
Neurogenic shock from cervical spine injury
(18.8%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has blunt chest trauma from a fall, with refractory hypotension and elevated central venous pressure despite fluid resuscitation, consistent with cardiogenic shock due to blunt cardiac injury rather than hypovolemic shock.
(Choice A)
Pericardial tamponade
Pericardial tamponade would present with similar findings of obstructive shock, elevated CVP, and refractory hypotension, but has been specifically excluded by bedside ultrasound showing no pericardial effusion.
(Choice B)
Tension pneumothorax
Tension pneumothorax would cause obstructive shock with elevated CVP and similar hemodynamics, but has been excluded by both chest x-ray and bedside ultrasound showing no pneumothorax.
(Choice C)
Neurogenic shock from cervical spine injury
Neurogenic shock from high cervical spine injury would typically present with the classic triad of hypotension, bradycardia, and warm dry skin due to loss of sympathetic tone. The tachycardia and elevated CVP in this patient are inconsistent with neurogenic shock.
(Choice D)
Hypovolemic shock from splenic laceration
This would typically present with low CVP due to volume loss, not elevated CVP as seen in this patient.
(Choice E)
Blunt cardiac injury
Blunt trauma can cause myocardial contusion leading to cardiogenic shock with elevated CVP and refractory hypotension despite fluids.

pages.question:
A 54-year-old woman presents with increasing lethargy and frequent dizzy spells. She has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes and is managed with oral antihypertensives and metformin. Recently, she began receiving hemodialysis following progression to end-stage renal disease. On her current regimen, she started erythropoietin therapy due to anemia (initial hemoglobin level was 8.1 g/dL). During the examination, her skin appears pale and dry. New lab results reveal: 

Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL
MCV 76 fL
MCHC 29 g/dL
WBC count 6,800/mm³
Platelets 148,000/mm³
Hemoglobin A1c 7.1%
ESR 14 mm/hr

What intervention would most likely alleviate this patient’s symptoms?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Erythropoietin therapy stimulates red blood cell production in CKD patients, but rapidly depletes iron stores due to increased demand for hemoglobin synthesis. This functional iron deficiency manifests as microcytic anemia despite erythropoietin treatment. Iron supplementation (typically intravenous) is essential to restore adequate iron availability for erythropoiesis.
(Choice A)
Optimization of blood pressure control
Managing blood pressure may prevent further renal deterioration but doesn't directly address anemia caused by reduced erythropoietin production.
(Choice B)
Parathyroidectomy
Parathyroidectomy can improve symptoms associated with secondary hyperparathyroidism in kidney disease, but it has no role in managing anemia.
(Choice C)
Increased erythropoietin dosage
Increasing erythropoietin dosage alone is ineffective when iron deficiency is present. Iron is an essential cofactor for hemoglobin synthesis, and without adequate iron stores, even optimal erythropoietin levels cannot effectively stimulate red blood cell production.
(Choice D)
Iron therapy
The anemia caused by chronic kidney disease is related to lower erythropoiesis due to insufficient erythropoietin. The resultant iron usage from increased RBC production after erythropoietin therapy can deplete iron stores, leading to microcytic anemia. Addressing the deficiency with intravenous iron, such as iron sucrose, can improve this condition.
(Choice E)
Vitamin B12 and folate supplementation
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia (MCV >100 fL), not microcytic anemia. This patient's MCV of 76 fL indicates microcytic anemia, which is characteristic of iron deficiency.

pages.question: A 52-year-old female elementary school teacher presents with a 3-month history of swelling in her left lower leg. She reports that the swelling is minimal in the morning but progressively worsens by the end of her workday, especially after standing for prolonged periods while teaching. The edema improves significantly after she elevates her legs in the evening or overnight while sleeping. She denies any pain, redness, or warmth in the leg, and there is no history of trauma, recent surgery, or prolonged immobility. On examination, there is 2+ pitting edema from the left ankle to mid-calf, with mild varicose veins visible on the posterior calf. The right leg is unaffected. Doppler ultrasound shows no evidence of deep vein thrombosis. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has unilateral lower extremity edema that worsens with prolonged standing and improves with elevation and recumbency overnight. This presentation is classic for venous valvular incompetence, the most common cause of such edema. Other etiologies like deep vein thrombosis or lymphedema are less likely given the absence of risk factors, negative ultrasound, and the positional nature of the symptoms.
(Choice A)
Congestive heart failure
This typically causes bilateral edema and is associated with other systemic symptoms like dyspnea, which are not present in this unilateral case.
(Choice B)
Venous valve incompetence
This is the most likely cause, as the symptoms worsen with dependency due to gravitational effects on impaired venous return and improve with elevation, consistent with chronic venous insufficiency.
(Choice C)
Chronic kidney disease
This leads to generalized edema due to hypoalbuminemia, not isolated unilateral lower extremity swelling that varies with position.
(Choice D)
Deep vein thrombosis
While DVT can cause unilateral edema, it typically presents acutely with pain, warmth, and erythema. The chronic, positional nature of symptoms and negative Doppler ultrasound definitively rule out acute thrombosis.
(Choice E)
Cellulitis
This infectious cause would present with erythema, warmth, pain, and systemic signs like fever, none of which are described.

pages.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to your clinic for pre-conception counseling. She is currently on a number of different medications and is concerned about their potential effects on pregnancy. She is planning to start a family in the near future. Her current medications include divalproex sodium, spironolactone, doxycycline, and levothyroxine. She has been on her current regimen for the past 3 years without any significant issues. She doesn't smoke or consume alcohol. Physical examination reveals a healthy female with stable vital signs. Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate for this patient?

answers.text:
Recommend switching divalproex sodium to another agent
(42.97%)

Recommend stopping doxycycline and continuing others
(14.84%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Pre-conception counseling requires careful evaluation of medication teratogenicity. Valproic acid poses the highest risk (up to 10-fold increased neural tube defects) and requires gradual transition to safer alternatives like lamotrigine under specialist supervision. Other teratogenic medications like spironolactone and doxycycline should also be discontinued before conception.
(Choice A)
Recommend continuing all current medications
This is inappropriate because multiple medications pose fetal risks: valproic acid significantly increases neural tube defect risk, spironolactone can cause feminization of male fetuses, and doxycycline causes teeth discoloration and bone development issues in the fetus.
(Choice B)
Recommend switching divalproex sodium to another agent
Valproic acid is the most teratogenic medication in this patient's regimen, carrying up to a 10-fold increased risk of neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly) as well as cognitive impairment and other structural malformations. In pre-conception counseling, transitioning valproic acid to a safer antiepileptic drug — such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam, which have more favorable fetal safety profiles — is the single most critical recommendation. This transition must be done gradually under neurology supervision to avoid breakthrough seizures, ideally 3–6 months before conception. High-dose folic acid (4–5 mg/day) should also be started. While spironolactone (fetal feminization) and doxycycline (teeth discoloration, bone development) must also be discontinued before conception, valproic acid's magnitude of teratogenic risk makes it the priority.
(Choice C)
Advise stopping levothyroxine
Levothyroxine is crucial for maintaining normal thyroid function and avoiding adverse pregnancy outcomes. Discontinuing it could lead to maternal and fetal complications.
(Choice D)
Suggest stopping spironolactone and doxycycline
While this approach addresses two problematic medications (spironolactone can cause feminization of male fetuses, and doxycycline causes teeth discoloration and bone growth issues), it fails to address the most significant teratogenic risk from valproic acid, which carries up to a 10-fold increased risk of neural tube defects.
(Choice E)
Recommend stopping doxycycline and continuing others
While doxycycline should be avoided in pregnancy due to teeth discoloration and bone development issues in the fetus, this approach fails to address the most significant teratogenic risk from valproic acid, which increases neural tube defect risk up to 10-fold.

pages.question:
A 32-year-old woman who recently tested positive for latent tuberculosis infection is started on isoniazid prophylaxis. Two months later, she presents with fatigue, nausea, and jaundice. Laboratory value are shown below. A liver biopsy shows lobular inflammation, hepatocellular necrosis, and scattered acidophil bodies, mimicking the histological pattern of acute viral hepatitis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?



White Blood Cell Count	7800 /mm³
Hemoglobin	14 g/dL
Hematocrit	42 %
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)	90 fL
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)	30 pg
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)	33 g/dL
Platelet Count	260000 /μL
Neutrophils	60 %
Lymphocytes	30 %
Monocytes	6 %
Eosinophils	3 %
Basophils	1 %
AST	650 U/L
ALT	720 U/L
Alkaline Phosphatase	100 U/L
Total Bilirubin	3.5 mg/dL
Direct Bilirubin	1.5 mg/dL
Albumin	3.8 g/dL
Hepatitis A Serology	Negative
Hepatitis B Serology	Negative
Hepatitis C Serology	Negative
Hepatitis E Serology	Negative
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient developed acute liver injury with jaundice and markedly elevated transaminases shortly after initiating isoniazid for latent TB. Negative viral serologies and biopsy findings consistent with viral-like hepatitis point to an idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury caused by isoniazid.
(Choice A)
Alcoholic steatohepatitis
There is no history of alcohol use, and the biopsy features are more consistent with viral-like hepatitis rather than steatohepatitis.
(Choice B)
Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis presents with cholestatic enzyme elevation (elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT), characteristic florid duct lesions on biopsy, and positive antimitochondrial antibodies. The predominantly hepatocellular injury pattern (AST/ALT >>ALP) and acute lobular hepatitis histology are inconsistent with PBC.
(Choice C)
Acute hepatitis A infection
Hepatitis A is ruled out by negative serologies. Additionally, the temporal relationship with isoniazid initiation 2 months prior strongly suggests drug-induced etiology rather than viral hepatitis.
(Choice D)
Hepatitis secondary to isoniazid usage
Isoniazid is known to cause idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury with histological features mimicking viral hepatitis, fitting the clinical timeline, negative viral tests, and biopsy findings.
(Choice E)
Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis typically presents with interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis) and prominent plasma cell infiltration on biopsy, contrasting with the lobular inflammation pattern described. Additionally, autoimmune hepatitis would require positive autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, or anti-LKM1) and typically has a more indolent course.

pages.question: A 28-year-old patient assigned female at birth presents to their primary care physician expressing a strong, persistent identification as male, which has been present for over a year. The patient reports significant distress, including anxiety and depression, that has led to difficulties maintaining employment and social relationships. They express a desire to pursue gender-affirming treatments but are unsure where to start. The patient denies any suicidal ideation and has no history of self-harm. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management approach?

answers.text:
Offer multidisciplinary support services and care
(96.43%)

Refer for psychiatric evaluation to confirm the patient is not experiencing a psychotic disorder
(3.57%)

Recommend immediate surgical consultation for gender-affirming genital reconstruction
(0%)

Reassure the patient that these feelings are likely transient and will resolve with time
(0%)

Initiate testosterone therapy immediately without further evaluation
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Gender dysphoria involves persistent (≥6 months) incongruence between assigned and experienced gender identity, with associated distress or functional impairment. Initial management focuses on safety assessment, providing nonjudgmental support, and coordinating multidisciplinary care. Treatment decisions regarding hormones or surgery require comprehensive evaluation, informed consent, and ongoing specialist collaboration following established clinical guidelines.
(Choice A)
Offer multidisciplinary support services and care
This is the correct initial approach, involving nonjudgmental support, safety assessment, and referral to a team of specialists for tailored treatment.
(Choice B)
Refer for psychiatric evaluation to confirm the patient is not experiencing a psychotic disorder
Gender dysphoria is not a psychiatric disorder to be 'ruled out' but rather a recognized condition requiring supportive care. While mental health evaluation is part of comprehensive care, approaching it from a pathologizing perspective is inappropriate and potentially harmful to the therapeutic relationship.
(Choice C)
Recommend immediate surgical consultation for gender-affirming genital reconstruction
Surgical options require extensive evaluation and are not an initial step; multidisciplinary assessment must precede such decisions.
(Choice D)
Reassure the patient that these feelings are likely transient and will resolve with time
This dismisses the patient's persistent distress and incongruence, which meets criteria for gender dysphoria, and does not provide appropriate support or referral.
(Choice E)
Initiate testosterone therapy immediately without further evaluation
Hormone therapy initiation requires comprehensive medical evaluation, informed consent processes, and baseline laboratory studies. Starting treatment immediately without proper assessment bypasses essential safety protocols and individualized care planning.

pages.question:
A 42-year-old woman with a history of recurrent acute pancreatitis due to hypertriglyceridemia presents to her physician with a 4-month history of fatigue, unintentional weight loss of 8 kg, and frequent bulky, oily stools that are difficult to flush. She reports increased bruising and dry, scaly skin on her extremities. She denies abdominal pain or changes in bowel habits prior to this period. Physical examination shows temporal wasting and ecchymoses on her arms. Laboratory values are shown below. Which of the following diagnostic findings is most consistent with this patient's condition?

Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL
Hematocrit 41 %                                  
Red blood cell count 4.7 x10^6/µL                
Mean corpuscular volume 90 fL                    
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin 30 pg                
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 34 g/dL
White blood cell count 7200 /mm³                 
Neutrophils 60 %                                 
Lymphocytes 30 %                                 
Monocytes 6 %                                    
Eosinophils 3 %                                  
Basophils 1 %                                    
Platelet count 250000 /µL                        
Random blood glucose 165 mg/dL                   
Serum vitamin A 25 µg/dL                         
Serum vitamin K 0.1 ng/mL
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency, presenting with steatorrhea, weight loss, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, and signs like bruising and dry skin. The hallmark diagnostic finding is decreased fecal elastase, confirming pancreatic exocrine dysfunction. Other choices do not align with the primary pathophysiology of pancreatic insufficiency.
(Choice A)
Decreased fecal elastase
Decreased fecal elastase is the most sensitive and specific noninvasive test for diagnosing pancreatic exocrine insufficiency in chronic pancreatitis, directly reflecting reduced pancreatic enzyme secretion.
(Choice B)
Elevated fecal calprotectin
Elevated fecal calprotectin indicates intestinal inflammation, typically seen in inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis. While IBD can occasionally cause malabsorption, it would not explain this patient's history of recurrent pancreatitis, selective fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, or diabetes mellitus.
(Choice C)
Increased serum trypsinogen
Serum trypsinogen levels are typically low in chronic pancreatitis due to acinar cell destruction, not increased; elevated levels might suggest acute inflammation.
(Choice D)
Decreased serum ceruloplasmin
Decreased serum ceruloplasmin is associated with Wilson disease, which can cause liver issues but not typically pancreatic insufficiency or steatorrhea.
(Choice E)
Positive anti-transglutaminase IgA
Positive anti-transglutaminase IgA suggests celiac disease, which can cause malabsorption and steatorrhea. However, celiac disease typically presents with broader nutrient deficiencies (iron, folate, B12) rather than selective fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, and is not associated with recurrent pancreatitis or diabetes mellitus as seen in this patient.

pages.question: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her caregiver after allegedly spilling hot soup on her hands while reaching for a bowl on the counter. Physical examination reveals symmetric circumferential burns on both hands and wrists, with a clear horizontal demarcation line at the mid-forearm level. The burns appear to be of uniform depth without any irregular patterns. Which of the following findings would most strongly indicate that this injury is non-accidental?

answers.text:
Varying depths of burns on the hands
(10.19%)

Presence of splash marks on the forearms
(3.7%)

Asymmetric involvement of only one hand
(2.78%)

Sparing of flexural creases at the wrists
(75.93%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Child abuse in the form of deliberate scald injuries is characterized by burns with sharp lines of demarcation, uniform depth, lack of splash marks, and spared flexural creases.
(Choice A)
Varying depths of burns on the hands
Varying burn depths indicate uneven exposure typical of accidents, where hot liquid may pool differently or contact skin for varying durations. Uniform depth suggests controlled, sustained contact with hot water as occurs in deliberate immersion abuse.
(Choice B)
Presence of splash marks on the forearms
Splash marks would suggest an accidental spill rather than deliberate immersion. In non-accidental immersion burns, the lack of splash marks is characteristic because the child's hands are held directly in hot water without the chaotic patterns of accidental spills.
(Choice C)
Asymmetric involvement of only one hand
Asymmetric burns are more likely accidental, while symmetric, bilateral involvement raises suspicion for non-accidental injury.
(Choice D)
Sparing of flexural creases at the wrists
Sparing of flexural creases is a hallmark of deliberate immersion burns in child abuse, as these areas are protected when the limb is flexed during forced submersion.
(Choice E)
Irregular, wavy burn margins
Irregular margins are more consistent with accidental burns from spills, where hot liquid flows unpredictably over skin. In contrast, non-accidental immersion burns create sharp, horizontal demarcation lines where the skin meets the hot water surface.

pages.question:
A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic with a 10-day history of severe left ear pain, purulent discharge, and progressive hearing loss. He reports no recent swimming or ear trauma but mentions frequent use of cotton swabs for cleaning. On physical examination, there is tenderness over the mastoid, granulation tissue visible in the external auditory canal, and subtle left-sided facial droop. Laboratory findings are shown below. Imaging with CT shows soft tissue swelling in the external canal with early erosion of the adjacent temporal bone. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient's condition? 



Hemoglobin	14.2 g/dL
Hematocrit	43%
WBC	7.100/mm³
Platelets	255.000/mm³
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)	48 mm/hr
Blood Glucose	185 mg/dL
Antinuclear Antibody (ANA)	Negative
Anti-dsDNA	Negative
Anti-Smith (Sm)	Negative
Anti-Ro (SSA)	Negative
Anti-La (SSB)	Negative
Rheumatoid Factor (RF)	Negative
Anti-CCP (Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide)	Negative
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa, a severe Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection extending to the skull base, commonly seen in elderly diabetics. The best initial treatment is intravenous ciprofloxacin for optimal coverage and penetration.
(Choice A)
Surgical debridement alone
While surgical debridement may be necessary as adjunctive therapy in cases with extensive necrotic tissue or treatment failure, systemic antimicrobial therapy targeting Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the cornerstone of initial management for necrotizing otitis externa. Surgery alone cannot eradicate the underlying infection.
(Choice B)
Intravenous vancomycin
While intravenous vancomycin provides excellent gram-positive coverage including MRSA, it has no activity against gram-negative organisms, particularly Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is the predominant pathogen in necrotizing otitis externa in diabetic patients.
(Choice C)
Intravenous ciprofloxacin
Intravenous ciprofloxacin is the first-line therapy for necrotizing otitis externa due to its excellent activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and good tissue penetration.
(Choice D)
Oral cephalexin
Oral cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin with primarily gram-positive coverage and lacks reliable activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the causative organism in necrotizing otitis externa. Additionally, oral antibiotics provide insufficient tissue penetration for this invasive skull base infection.
(Choice E)
Topical neomycin-polymyxin drops
Topical antibiotic drops are appropriate for uncomplicated otitis externa but are inadequate for necrotizing otitis externa, which involves deep tissue invasion and osteomyelitis of the skull base. The infection requires systemic intravenous antibiotics with good bone penetration and anti-Pseudomonas activity.

pages.question:
A 30-year-old man with a history of cryptorchidism corrected in childhood presents to the urology clinic after noticing a painless swelling in his right testicle over the past month. He reports no trauma, fever, or urinary symptoms, and his medical history is otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination reveals a firm, nontender, 2 cm mass within the right testicular parenchyma. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrates a solid, hypoechoic intratesticular lesion. Lab values are shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?



Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	41%
Red Blood Cell Count	4.7 million/μL
Mean Corpuscular Volume	88 fL
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin	29 pg
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration	33 g/dL
Red Cell Distribution Width	12.5%
White Blood Cell Count	7200/mm³
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	7%
Eosinophils	2%
Basophils	1%
Platelet Count	250000/mm³
Alpha Fetoprotein	60 ng/mL	0 to 40 ng/mL
Beta hCG	4 mIU/mL	<2 mIU/mL
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's history of cryptorchidism significantly increases his risk for testicular cancer, and the clinical presentation of a solid, firm, nontender testicular mass with supportive ultrasound findings and elevated tumor markers (AFP 60 ng/mL, mildly elevated beta-hCG) strongly suggests malignancy. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the standard of care as it provides both definitive histologic diagnosis and initial treatment while preserving normal lymphatic drainage patterns for accurate staging. Transscrotal approaches are contraindicated due to risk of tumor seeding and alteration of lymphatic pathways.
(Choice A)
Transscrotal fine-needle aspiration biopsy
Transscrotal needle biopsy is contraindicated because it violates the scrotal wall and risks tumor seeding along the needle tract, potentially altering lymphatic drainage patterns and complicating subsequent staging and treatment.
(Choice B)
Radical inguinal orchiectomy
Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the correct next step, providing both definitive diagnosis via pathology and initial treatment while preserving appropriate lymphatic pathways for staging.
(Choice C)
Observation with serial ultrasounds
Observation with serial ultrasounds is inappropriate for a solid testicular mass in a patient with risk factors (cryptorchidism history) and abnormal tumor markers, as delay in treatment of testicular cancer can lead to disease progression and worse outcomes.
(Choice D)
Initiate systemic chemotherapy
Systemic chemotherapy is inappropriate as the initial management because it requires histologic confirmation of malignancy, determination of tumor histology, and proper staging before treatment selection. Orchiectomy provides both diagnosis and initial treatment.
(Choice E)
Fine-needle aspiration of the mass
Fine-needle aspiration is not recommended due to the risk of tumor dissemination and inadequate tissue sampling for accurate diagnosis.

pages.question: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 20 weeks' gestation comes for an antenatal check-up. She has felt generally well, apart from some mild morning sickness earlier in her pregnancy. She reports no urinary symptoms such as dysuria or frequency, and she has no history of urinary infections. She is currently taking prenatal vitamins. She denies tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use. Her vital signs include a temperature of 36.8°C, blood pressure of 118/76 mm Hg, and a pulse rate of 72/min. Upon examination, her abdominal shape is consistent with her gestational age, and no notable abnormalities are found. A clean-catch urine sample reveals a colony count over 100,000 CFU/mL of Enterococcus species. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Perform a repeat culture in 2 weeks
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy requires immediate antibiotic treatment to prevent serious maternal and fetal complications including pyelonephritis, preterm labor, and low birth weight. Treatment selection must consider both antimicrobial effectiveness against the specific pathogen and pregnancy safety. For Enterococcus species, ampicillin (if sensitive) or nitrofurantoin are preferred first-line agents. A 7-day course is standard for asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy.
(Choice A)
Amoxicillin for 7 days
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy requires immediate antibiotic treatment to prevent progression to pyelonephritis, preterm labor, and low birth weight. Enterococcus faecalis, the most common Enterococcus species causing urinary tract infections, is typically susceptible to amoxicillin/ampicillin, making amoxicillin for 7 days an appropriate first-line regimen when susceptibility is confirmed. Nitrofurantoin for 7 days is an equally valid alternative. Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy, and a 3-day course of any agent is insufficient for asymptomatic bacteriuria — 7 days is the recommended duration. Follow-up culture 1–2 weeks after treatment completion confirms eradication.
(Choice B)
Monitor with no intervention
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy must be treated to prevent serious complications including pyelonephritis, preterm labor, and low birth weight. The 'wait and see' approach is inappropriate given the significant maternal and fetal risks.
(Choice C)
Levofloxacin for 3 days
Fluoroquinolones like levofloxacin are contraindicated during pregnancy due to potential risks including fetal cartilage and joint damage. Additionally, a 3-day course is inadequate for treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy, which requires 7 days of treatment.
(Choice D)
Nitrofurantoin for 3 days
While nitrofurantoin is a preferred treatment in pregnancy, a 3-day regimen is insufficient. A full 7-day course is necessary for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
(Choice E)
Perform a repeat culture in 2 weeks
While follow-up culture is important after treatment, delaying antibiotic therapy for 2 weeks allows progression to symptomatic UTI or pyelonephritis, which poses significant risks to both mother and fetus. Immediate treatment is indicated.

pages.question: A 9-year-old girl is taken to the pediatric clinic by her parents due to a worsening fever, sore throat, and a distinctive red rash. She has been complaining of throat pain over the past 3 days. Her medical history shows no significant illness and her immunizations records are current. Upon examination, her vital signs are a fever of 38.5°C (101.3°F), tachycardia with a pulse of 110/min, and normal blood pressure. The physical examination reveals a widespread erythematous rash with a rough texture covering her back and abdomen, which blanches upon pressing. Her plus-sized tonsils are red and covered with a whitish exudate, and there is palpable neck lymphadenopathy. Based on the clinical presentation, what is the most probable diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The case describes a girl with a history and physical examination that strongly suggests scarlet fever. The association with Group A Streptococcal infection and the sandpaper-like rash following pharyngitis are classic indicators. Understanding the distinct clinical presentation helps differentiate it from other rash-related illnesses in pediatrics, emphasizing the importance of targeted antibiotic therapy to prevent complications.
(Choice A)
Roseola
Roseola (HHV-6 infection) typically affects children 6 months to 2 years old. It presents with 3-4 days of high fever without other symptoms, followed by defervescence and appearance of a maculopapular rash. The concurrent fever and rash, plus the patient's age, make roseola unlikely.
(Choice B)
Measles
Measles typically presents with the 4 Cs: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots (pathognomonic blue-white spots on buccal mucosa). The rash appears 2-4 days after fever onset, starting at the hairline and spreading downward. The absence of these classic prodromal symptoms and the rough-textured rash make measles unlikely.
(Choice C)
Toxic shock syndrome
Toxic shock syndrome presents with high fever, hypotension (a key diagnostic criterion), and multi-organ dysfunction. The rash is typically diffuse erythroderma that later desquamates, not the rough sandpaper texture described. The absence of hypotension and multi-system involvement makes TSS unlikely.
(Choice D)
Mumps
Mumps presents with painful parotid gland swelling (parotitis), often unilateral initially. While fever may occur, mumps does not cause the characteristic sandpaper rash or exudative pharyngitis seen in this patient. The absence of parotid swelling makes mumps unlikely.
(Choice E)
Scarlet fever
The girl's symptoms align with scarlet fever. The condition is caused by Group A Streptococcus, associated with a characteristic sandpaper-textured rash, fever, and pharyngitis. Antibiotic therapy is crucial for management.

pages.question: A 32-year-old woman with a history of epilepsy gives birth to a full-term male infant. The mother reports compliance with her prescribed antiepileptic medication throughout pregnancy. Physical examination of the newborn reveals microcephaly, a notably wide anterior fontanelle, cleft lip and palate, and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges in both hands. Which of the following maternal medications is most likely responsible for these findings?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This infant most likely has fetal hydantoin syndrome, which occurs due to in utero exposure to antiepileptics such as phenytoin. It is characterized by cleft lip and palate, wide anterior fontanelle, distal phalange hypoplasia, and microcephaly.
(Choice A)
Isotretinoin
Isotretinoin (retinoic acid embryopathy) causes craniofacial malformations, cardiac defects, and CNS abnormalities including microtia, cleft palate, and neural tube defects. However, the specific triad of wide anterior fontanelle, distal phalangeal hypoplasia, and the overall pattern described is characteristic of fetal hydantoin syndrome, not isotretinoin exposure.
(Choice B)
Phenytoin
Phenytoin exposure in utero can cause fetal hydantoin syndrome, featuring microcephaly, wide anterior fontanelle, cleft lip/palate, and distal phalange hypoplasia.
(Choice C)
Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is generally considered safer in pregnancy with lower teratogenic risk and does not typically cause the constellation of findings seen in fetal hydantoin syndrome.
(Choice D)
Valproic acid
Valproic acid causes fetal valproate syndrome, characterized by neural tube defects (spina bifida), distinctive facial features (thin upper lip, broad nasal bridge, epicanthal folds), and developmental delays. Unlike fetal hydantoin syndrome, it does not typically cause cleft lip/palate or the specific pattern of distal phalangeal hypoplasia seen in this case.
(Choice E)
Warfarin
Warfarin embryopathy (fetal warfarin syndrome) occurs with first-trimester exposure and includes nasal hypoplasia with a flattened nasal bridge, stippled epiphyses on radiographs, and congenital heart defects. The constellation of microcephaly, wide anterior fontanelle, cleft lip/palate, and distal phalangeal hypoplasia is not seen with warfarin exposure.

pages.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist with infertility after attempting to conceive for 12 months without success. She reports irregular menstrual cycles occurring every 35-45 days and has noticed increased facial hair growth and acne over the past few years. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m² and her blood pressure is 125/85 mmHg. Laboratory evaluation is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?



WBC Count	7100 /µL
Neutrophils	60 %
Lymphocytes	30 %
Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	40 %
RBC Count	4.6 million/µL
Platelet Count	250000 /µL
Serum 17-Hydroxyprogesterone	250 ng/dL
Testosterone	400 ng/dL
Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulfate (DHEA-S)	180 µg/dL
Sodium	140 mEq/L
Potassium	4.2 mEq/L
Chloride	103 mEq/L
Bicarbonate (HCO3-)	24 mEq/L
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to partial 21-hydroxylase deficiency, presenting with hyperandrogenism (irregular menses, hirsutism, acne, infertility) and significantly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone (>200 ng/dL), with normal electrolytes and blood pressure distinguishing it from classic CAH.
(Choice A)
Premature ovarian insufficiency
Premature ovarian insufficiency causes irregular menses and infertility due to estrogen deficiency, with elevated FSH levels, but it does not feature hyperandrogenism or elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
(Choice B)
Androgen-secreting ovarian tumor
Androgen-secreting ovarian tumors cause severe hyperandrogenism with markedly elevated testosterone levels and often virilization. While this patient has elevated testosterone (400 ng/dL, normal <70 ng/dL), the specific elevation of 17-hydroxyprogesterone points to an adrenal rather than ovarian source.
(Choice C)
Polycystic ovary syndrome
PCOS typically presents with hyperandrogenism and irregular menses but usually has normal or only mildly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels (<200 ng/dL in follicular phase). The significantly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone (250 ng/dL) in this case points to a different diagnosis.
(Choice D)
Nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to partial 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents with hyperandrogenism (eg, hirsutism, acne, irregular menses, infertility) and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels, with normal electrolytes and blood pressure, matching this patient's presentation.
(Choice E)
Idiopathic hirsutism
Idiopathic hirsutism involves increased hair growth without identifiable cause, but it does not typically cause irregular menses, infertility, or elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels.

pages.question:
A 62-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease secondary to diabetic nephropathy has been on hemodialysis for 14 years. She presents with a 6-month history of worsening bilateral shoulder pain and noticeable swelling around the shoulders, described as a 'shoulder pad' appearance. She also reports numbness and tingling in both hands, particularly at night, with weakness in gripping objects. Physical examination reveals limited range of motion in the shoulders and positive Tinel's sign at the wrists. Laboratory studies are shown below. Radiographs of the shoulders demonstrate cystic lesions in the humeral heads. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?



White blood cell count	8200/mm3
Neutrophils	58%
Lymphocytes	32%
Monocytes	7%
Eosinophils	2%
